newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Prices seen remaining contained.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK--Prices seen remaining contained.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities weren't seen moving sharply on Thursday as the market would have little new information on which to trade.
Initial unemployment claims, seen dropping to 334,000 in the week ended April May 3 from 347,000 the prior week, were the only data scheduled.

The Federal Reserve reported on Wednesday that the economy expanded moderately over the past two months with wages and retail prices subdued. In its Beige Book report, the Fed said labot market conditions remained tight.

"We expected to see more wage pressure in the Beige Book report, but while labor conditions remain tight there's little evidence of wage inflation," said Mark Vitner, economist with First Union Corp's capital markets group.

The economy continued to improve and the budget deficit also was in better shape, Vitner said. There was some slowing expected in the economy but production remained strong and didn't seem set to slow, he said.
With demand strong and inventories lean, the only wild card was striking automobile industry workers that could slow output, he said.
Vitner said production would have to increase in the immediate future in order to meet demand.
"There's a real split in opinion on whether the economy is gaining or losing momentum," Vitner said. With the budget situation clarified, he saw no fiscal drag going forward.
The Treasury's auction of 10-year notes on Wednesday was weak, following a poor three-year sale on Tuesday. That helped to put a damper on Treasury prices.
The Federal Reserve raised short-term interest rates by 25 basis points at its last policy-making meeting on March 25 and another hike was expected by many analysts.

Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin on Wednesday expressed worry that the tight labor market could lead to increased wage and price inflation. But she said no signs of inflation had been detected yet and economic growth remained strong.
Richard Berner, executive vice president and chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp, said the market was waiting to see more information about inflation before moving further.
"There was a stunning rally last week but the realization has set in that the budget accord was not all it seemed to be," said Berner.
"There's a dispute about just how much of a reduction we're going to see. We're seeing only the bare bones of a deal," Berner said.

He added that there still was uncertainty about how strong U.S. economic growth has been in the second quarter. Nonetheless, he expected the Fed would move to raise interest rates at its next meeting on May 20.
It would have to be seen how much auto workers' strikes had impacted initial claims in order to get a clearer reading on the strength of the labor market, Berner said.
The 30-year Treasury bond was trading at 95-25/32 late Wednesday, yielding 6.96 percent.
Three-month bills were up five basis points to 5.10 percent. Six-month bills were down one basis point at 5.34 percent and year bills were up five basis points at 5.61 percent.
Two-year notes down 4/32 at 100-01/32 to yield 6.36 percent. Five-year notes were off 11/32 to 99/-30/32 to yield 6.64 percent and 10-years were down 20/32 at 96-13/32 to yield 6.76 percent.
